title: Joshua 2:1–7
context: From Shittim, Israel’s camp east of the Jordan, Joshua secretly sends two men to view the land, including Jericho. They enter the house of a prostitute named Rahab and lodge there. The king of Jericho hears of them and demands that Rahab bring the men out. She hides them and tells the king’s messengers that the visitors came, but that she did not know where they were from and that they left at dark when the gate was shutting. The narrator then shows that she had taken them to the roof and hidden them under stalks of flax. The pursuers head toward the fords of the Jordan, and the city gate is shut. Both traditions take the unit as the opening of Rahab’s story, which will shortly become a confession of the LORD and a request for mercy. The herem against Jericho has not yet begun. The ethics of her deception are debated inside both traditions rather than along a single Arminian–Reformed line. Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25 later commend her faith and her receiving of the messengers.

verses.text: Joshua the son of Nun secretly sent two men out of Shittim as spies, saying, “Go, view the land, including Jericho.” They went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab, and slept there.
verses.arminianNotes:
From Shittim Joshua secretly sends two men to view the land, including Jericho. They enter the house of “a prostitute whose name was Rahab” and sleep there.

Arminian readers hear an ordinary, even risky, human mission. The men lodge in an unexpected house, and the narrator names Rahab’s trade without softening it; God can still work through her, as the next scene will show.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take Shittim as the sending point east of the Jordan and Rahab as the text names her. “slept there” reports that they lodged in her house; the story does not pause to charge or clear them of further sin, and its interest is the mission and the woman God will use.

Both traditions refuse to recast her as something other than what the text, and later New Testament witnesses, call her, and they wait for her confession in the verses that follow.

verses.text: The king of Jericho was told, “Behold, men of the children of Israel came in here tonight to spy out the land.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Jericho is told, “Behold, men of the children of Israel came in here tonight to spy out the land.” The secret mission is already known in the city.

Arminian readers hear how quickly human secrecy fails. The spies’ danger is real, and the next verses will show a woman having to decide what to do with that danger.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the city’s king is alerted the same night. The LORD’s purpose is not tied to the success of concealment alone; the report sets the crisis in which Rahab will act.

Both traditions take the verse as the threat coming into the open, shared narrative ground.

verses.text: Jericho’s king sent to Rahab, saying, “Bring out the men who have come to you, who have entered into your house; for they have come to spy out all the land.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jericho’s king sends to Rahab and demands, “Bring out the men who have come to you, who have entered into your house; for they have come to spy out all the land.”

Arminian readers hear a direct royal order that puts Rahab to the test. She must now either hand the men over or refuse a king’s command, a real moral decision in her own night.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the king treats her house as the place of the spies and assumes her control over those who have entered it. The demand is official and public; her response will be decisive.

Both traditions read the summons as the pressure under which her coming words and actions take place.

verses.text: The woman took the two men and hid them. Then she said, “Yes, the men came to me, but I didn’t know where they came from.
verses.arminianNotes:
Rahab hides the two men, then says they came to her, but that she did not know where they came from. The narrator first tells us she hid them, then reports her answer to the king’s messengers.

Arminian readers do not treat the deception as a small thing. Whether her lie was a sin God nonetheless used, or a tragic choice under conflicting duties, is debated among Arminian readers themselves, as it is among others.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse to make this verse a party contrast. Some in the Reformed tradition have judged the lie sinful even while praising her faith; others have argued for a more tragic or wartime account. The text reports the hiding and the false report; it does not pause to theorize.

Both traditions agree that later Scripture commends her faith and her receiving of the spies, not a general license to deceive.

verses.text: About the time of the shutting of the gate, when it was dark, the men went out. Where the men went, I don’t know. Pursue them quickly. You may catch up with them.”
verses.arminianNotes:
She adds that the men went out about the time of the shutting of the gate, when it was dark, that she does not know where they went, and that the pursuers should go quickly if they hope to catch them.

Arminian readers hear a further, active misdirection. The ethical questions already noted in verse 4 continue here; the verse itself is her speech, and it is false.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the same detailed false trail: timing, darkness, a claimed departure, and an urging to pursue. The narrative will immediately show what she had actually done.

Both traditions read the speech as concealment of the spies, and they keep the moral debate about her words inside each tradition rather than along an Arminian–Reformed line.

verses.text: But she had brought them up to the roof, and hidden them under the stalks of flax which she had laid in order on the roof.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator now tells the truth: she had already brought the men to the roof and hidden them under stalks of flax laid out there. Her public story is exposed as a cover for this hiding.

Arminian readers hear the writer’s own account of the facts. The flax on the roof is a simple, domestic detail; her courage is in the hiding, which later Scripture will count among the works of her faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the narrator’s “But”: the men were never gone. The roof and the flax are the means of their protection, and the LORD’s purpose moves forward through this concealment.

Both traditions take the verse as the factual key to verses 4–5, without turning the flax itself into a forced symbol.

verses.text: The men pursued them along the way to the fords of the Jordan River. As soon as those who pursued them had gone out, they shut the gate.
verses.arminianNotes:
The pursuers go along the way to the fords of the Jordan River, and as soon as they have gone out, the gate is shut. The ruse works for the moment, and the spies are now sealed inside a closed city.

Arminian readers hear both deliverance and new danger. The pursuers are drawn away, yet the shut gate means the men cannot simply walk out; they will need Rahab’s further help.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the same closing of the gate. Human pursuit runs to the river, and the city’s ordinary night security now traps the spies inside—the setting for the conversation on the roof.

Both traditions take the verse as the chase leaving Jericho and the gate shutting, shared narrative ground.
